content: Patients who received less than 18 months of treatment, which was previously the minimum duration recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for longer regimens, were excluded from the analysis (N = 346). For PICO question 3 (MDR/RR-TB, 2018), when drug susceptibility testing (DST) results were available, a medication was deemed effective if the results indicated susceptibility. Conversely, it was not considered effective if resistance was observed. In cases where DST results were missing, two scenarios were considered: 1. If the prevalence of resistance to the medication was less than 10% in the same population (based on data from the same country or study site, or overall data if local information was unavailable), the medication was counted as effective. This applied to agents such as cycloserine or terizidone, linezolid, clofazimine, bedaquiline, carbapenems, and delamanid. 2. If the prevalence of resistance was 10% or higher in the same population, imputed DST results were used to determine effectiveness. If the imputed DST results showed susceptibility, the medication was considered effective; if resistance was shown, it was not. This applied to agents such as pyrazinamide, ethambutol, second-line injectable agents, fluoroquinolones, p-aminosalicylic acid, and ethionamide or prothionamide. Certain medications were excluded from the count of effective drugs regardless of DST results. These included isoniazid (including high-dose isoniazid), rifampicin, rifabutin, thioacetazone, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and macrolide antibiotics. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of addressing key subgroups, such as children, who were underrepresented in the 2018 individual patient data meta-analysis (IPD-MA). In the absence of pediatric data, evidence from adults was extrapolated to children. Recommendations were based on the best available evidence to design regimens with high relapse-free cure rates, reduced mortality, and minimized risk of additional resistance, while limiting harm. The GDG reviewed data from the 2016 pediatric MDR-TB IPD-MA, which included 975 cases of pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB. Children with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) were excluded due to the non-comparability of their treatment regimens and the small sample size (n = 36). No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the dataset, and the certainty of the evidence was judged to be very low. The GDG evaluated the contribution of individual drugs in longer MDR-TB regimens using data from the 2018 IPD-MA and Trial 213 (delamanid). Medications were categorized into three groups: Group A: Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin), bedaquiline, and linezolid were considered highly effective and strongly recommended for inclusion in all regimens unless contraindicated. Group B: Clofazimine and cycloserine or terizidone were conditionally recommended as second-choice agents. Group C: Other medications were included to complete the regimen when Group A and B agents could not be used. These were ranked by their relative benefit-to-harm balance. Kanamycin and capreomycin were associated with poorer outcomes and are no longer recommended for MDR-TB regimens. Gatifloxacin and high-dose isoniazid were used in very few patients, and thioacetazone was not used at all. Quality-assured preparations of gatifloxacin are unavailable due to concerns about dysglycemia, and thioacetazone is unlikely to play a role in contemporary regimens. High-dose isoniazid may be used in patients with confirmed susceptibility to isoniazid. Clavulanic acid should only be used as a companion to carbapenems (imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem) and is not counted as an additional effective TB agent. The GDG found insufficient evidence to make recommendations on perchlozone, interferon gamma, or sutezolid due to a lack of final patient outcome data. Regarding bedaquiline use in patients under 18 years, the GDG concluded that exposure-response profiles could be extrapolated from adults to children. Data from two trials (TMC207-C211 and IMPAACT P1108) indicated that doses evaluated in children aged 6–17 years did not increase the risk of treatment failure. Safety risks in children as young as 6 years were comparable to adults, though more data are needed before upgrading the recommendation to a strong one. For delamanid use in children under 6 years, the GDG recommended restricting extrapolations of efficacy and safety to children aged 3–5 years, based on pharmacological and safety data. Exposure profiles in children aged 3–5 years were comparable to adults and older children. However, concerns were raised about the feasibility of administering the correct dose to children aged 3–5 years, as the special 25 mg formulation used in trials is unavailable, and the adult 50 mg tablet is not bioequivalent. The GDG recommended that longer MDR-TB regimens include all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent, starting with at least four effective drugs. If only one or two Group A agents can be used, both Group B agents should be included. Group C agents are added if necessary to complete the regimen. Injectable agents should only be used if DST confirms susceptibility and high-quality audiometry monitoring is available. Streptomycin is considered only if amikacin cannot be used and DST confirms susceptibility.
